Israel defeats the people of Arad (verses 1–3)

Before Israel began traveling around Edom, the Canaanite king of Arad attacked the Israelites in the wilderness and captured some of them.

The incident was meant to lead the people to trust the Lord more completely.

The bronze serpent and the healing of Israel (verses 4–9)

Israel became exhausted by the long journey around Edom.

The people complained bitterly about what God had already done and distrusted what he might do next.

If manna could not satisfy them, what would?

We must not let other people's contempt for God's word make us value it less.

That word is the real Bread of Life.

It nourishes to eternal life everyone who receives it by faith, no matter who dismisses it as worthless.

God justly judged the people for their complaints by sending venomous serpents into the camp.

Many were bitten and died.

They might never have admitted their sin without first suffering from its consequences.

But suffering led them toward repentance.

God then provided a remarkable cure.

Henry observes that Jewish interpreters themselves explain that merely seeing the bronze serpent did not heal people.

Rather, by looking up at it, the sufferers were looking toward God, the One who healed them.

The act was filled with gospel meaning.

Jesus himself said that just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that those who believe in him will not perish (John 3:14–15).

Our sickness is like theirs: sin bites and poisons the soul.

Their cure pictured ours.

They looked and lived.

We believe in Jesus and do not perish.

Faith turns our eyes toward him (Hebrews 12:2).

Anyone who looked was healed, however severe the bite, weak the eyesight or distant the sufferer.

God can save us through means that human reasoning would never invent.

How different people would live if they felt the poison of the ancient serpent's temptation as clearly as Israel felt those bites!

If we truly recognized the eternal danger of sin, we would not close our eyes to Christ or turn away from his gospel.

We would count everything else as loss compared with a crucified Savior.

We would call on him without delay.

Nor would we abuse the generosity of Christ's salvation once we understood the price he paid to provide it.

Israel's journeys and the well of water (verses 10–20)

These verses describe Israel's movements until the people reached the plains of Moab, from which they would later cross the Jordan into Canaan.

The end of their journey was near.

It would be good for us, as we draw nearer to heaven, to grow more active and fruitful in the Lord's work.

The record also recalls God's extraordinary victories for Israel, including events around the River Arnon, Waheb in Suphah and neighboring places.

At every stage—and indeed every step—of life, we should remember what God has done for us.

We should recall distinctly the help he gave at particular times and places.

The Lord provided water, and Israel received it with joy and thanksgiving.

Their gratitude made the gift sweeter.

When we reach heaven, we will come to the fountain of living water.

Even now we should draw joy from the wells of salvation (Isaiah 12:3).

The bronze serpent pictured Christ lifted up to heal us.

The well pictured the Holy Spirit poured out to comfort us, from whom flow rivers of living water (John 7:38–39).

If that water is flowing within our souls, we should enjoy its comfort and give God all the praise.

God promised water, but the Israelites still had to open the ground to receive it.

We should expect his gifts while using the lawful means he has placed within our reach, remembering that all real power belongs to him.

Sihon and Og are defeated (verses 21–35)

Sihon led his forces outside his own borders against Israel without provocation.

In doing so, he brought about his own defeat.

Enemies of God's church often destroy themselves through the plans they consider most clever.

Og, king of Bashan, could have learned from Sihon's defeat and sought peace.

Instead he made war and suffered the same destruction.

Wicked people make enormous efforts to protect themselves and their possessions from God's judgment.

But when judgment comes, their precautions cannot save them.

God gave Israel victories while Moses was still alive.

Moses could witness the beginning of the great conquest even though he would not live to see it completed.

These early victories were small compared with what lay ahead, but they promised greater things.

Christians must prepare for new struggles and new enemies.

We should make no compromise with the powers of darkness, expecting no permanent ceasefire with them.

Trusting God and obeying his commands, we will overcome every spiritual enemy.

[Num.21.1-Num.21.3]
Chapter 21
Chapter Outline
The Canaanites of Arad destroyed. | (1-3) |
The people murmuring, are plagued with fiery serpents, They repenting, are healed through the brazen serpent. | (4-9) |
Further journeys of the Israelites. | (10-20) |
Sihon and Og overcome, Their land possessed. | (21-35) |
Verses 1-3
Before the people began their march round the country of Edom, the king of Arad, a Canaanite, who inhabited the southern part of the country, attacked them in the wilderness, and took some prisoners. This was to lead the Israelites to look more thoroughly to the Lord.
[Num.21.4-Num.21.9]
Verses 4-9
The children of Israel were wearied by a long march round the land of Edom. They speak discontentedly of what God had done for them, and distrustfully of what he would do. What will they be pleased with, whom manna will not please? Let not the contempt which some cast on the word of God, make us value it less. It is the bread of life, substantial bread, and will nourish those who by faith feed upon it, to eternal life, whoever may call it light bread. We see the righteous judgment God brought upon them for murmuring. He sent fiery serpents among them, which bit or stung many to death. It is to be feared that they would not have owned the sin, if they had not felt the smart; but they relent under the rod. And God made a wonderful provision for their relief. The Jews themselves say it was not the sight of the brazen serpent that cured; but in looking up to it, they looked up to God as the Lord that healed them. There was much gospel in this. Our Saviour declared, [John.3.14] Joh 3:14, [John.3.15] 15, that as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of man must be lifted up, that whatsoever believeth in him, should not perish. Compare their disease and ours. Sin bites like a serpent, and stings like an adder. Compare the application of their remedy and ours. They looked and lived, and we, if we believe, shall not perish. It is by faith that we look unto Jesus, [Heb.12.2] He 12:2. Whosoever looked, however desperate his case, or feeble his sight, or distant his place, was certainly and perfectly cured. The Lord can relieve us from dangers and distresses, by means which human reason never would have devised. Oh that the venom of the old serpent, inflaming men's passions, and causing them to commit sins which end in their eternal destruction, were as sensibly felt, and the danger as plainly seen, as the Israelites felt pain from the bite of the fiery serpents, and feared the death which followed! Then none would shut their eyes to Christ, or turn from his gospel. Then a crucified Saviour would be so valued, that all things else would be accounted loss for him; then, without delay, and with earnestness and simplicity, all would apply to him in the appointed way, crying, Lord, save us; we perish! Nor would any abuse the freeness of Christ's salvation, while they reckoned the price which it cost him.
[Num.21.10-Num.21.20]
Verses 10-20
We have here the removes of the children of Israel, till they came to the plains of Moab, from whence they passed over Jordan into Canaan. The end of their pilgrimage was near. "They set forward." It were well if we did thus; and the nearer we come to heaven, were so much the more active and abundant in the work of the Lord. The wonderful success God granted to his people, is here spoken of, and, among the rest, their actions on the river Arnon, at Vaheb in Suphah, and other places on that river. In every stage of our lives, nay, in every step, we should notice what God has wrought for us; what he did at such a time, and what in such a place, ought to be distinctly remembered. God blessed his people with a supply of water. When we come to heaven, we shall remove to the well of life, the fountain of living waters. They received it with joy and thankfulness, which made the mercy doubly sweet. With joy must we draw water out of the wells of salvation, [Isa.12.3] Is 12:3. As the brazen serpent was a figure of Christ, who is lifted up for our cure, so is this well a figure of the Spirit, who is poured forth for our comfort, and from whom flow to us rivers of living waters, [John.7.38] Joh 7:38, [John.7.39] 39. Does this well spring up in our souls? If so, we should take the comfort to ourselves, and give the glory to God. God promised to give water, but they must open the ground. God's favours must be expected in the use of such means as are within our power, but still the power is only of God.
[Num.21.21-Num.21.35]
Verses 21-35
Sihon went with his forces against Israel, out of his own borders, without provocation, and so ran upon his own ruin. The enemies of God's church often perish by the counsels they think most wisely taken. Og, king of Bashan, instead of being warned by the fate of his neighbours, to make peace with Israel, makes war with them, which proves in like manner his destruction. Wicked men do their utmost to secure themselves and their possessions against the judgments of God; but all in vain, when the day comes on which they must fall. God gave Israel success, while Moses was with them, that he might see the beginning of the glorious work, though he must not live to see it finished. This was, in comparison, but as the day of small things, yet it was an earnest of great things. We must prepare for fresh conflicts and enemies. We must make no peace or truce with the powers of darkness, nor even treat with them; nor should we expect any pause in our contest. But, trusting in God, and obeying his commands, we shall be more than conquerors over every enemy.

Balak asks Balaam to curse Israel (verses 1–14)

The king of Moab formed a plan to have Israel cursed.

He wanted God, who had been fighting for Israel, to turn against the people.

He mistakenly imagined that a prophet's curse against Israel—and a blessing upon his own army—would enable him to defeat them.

Balaam had a remarkable reputation, so Balak sent far away to hire him.

Henry says we do not know whether God had spoken to Balaam or through him before these events.

It seems possible, but afterward God certainly did speak through him.

Yet Scripture gives convincing evidence that Balaam lived and died as a wicked person and an enemy of God and his people.

A curse uttered against someone cannot harm that person without just cause.

Balak's messengers brought payment meant to tempt Balaam into wrongdoing.

But God restrained Balaam and forbade him to curse Israel.

Balaam was not ignorant of Israel's situation.

He should have answered immediately that he could never curse a people whom God had blessed.

Instead he delayed overnight to consider the proposal.

When we bargain with temptation, we place ourselves in danger.

Balaam did not faithfully communicate the full force of God's command to the messengers.

People who soften divine prohibitions are particularly vulnerable to temptation, treating disobedience as though it merely required additional permission.

The messengers also misrepresented Balaam's reply when reporting it to Balak.

Flattering advisers can keep rulers and other people from recognizing their own folly.

A second delegation persuades Balaam (verses 15–21)

Balak sent a second group of messengers.

How good it would be if we persevered so firmly in doing right even after disappointments!

Balak appealed both to Balaam's greed and to his pride and ambition.

We should pray continually for God to mortify such desires within us.

Sinners spare neither time, cost nor humiliation when pursuing luxury or malice.

Should believers be less willing to do what is good?

Balaam knew that he was obligated to obey God.

His public words sounded excellent.

But speaking religiously proves nothing about the actual condition of the heart.

Many call God their Lord without truly belonging to him.

Balaam seemed to reject the offer, but he never expressed genuine hatred for the proposed sin.

He wanted the reward and hoped to receive God's permission to do what was already forbidden.

A heart is ruled by corruption when it asks God for permission to sin.

God left Balaam to pursue his own desires.

Just as God sometimes denies his children's requests in love, he may grant sinful desires in judgment.

The angel opposes Balaam on the road (verses 22–35)

God sometimes permits people to proceed in sin.

We must never interpret that permission as approval.

Holy angels oppose wrongdoing and may prevent more of it than we realize.

The angel was Balaam's adversary only because Balaam was pursuing the wrong road.

People who block our progress toward sin are often our truest friends.

God exposed his displeasure to Balaam through the donkey.

A person determined to do evil may force a way forward despite every warning placed in the path by Providence.

The Lord made the animal speak.

This was a real miracle of God's power.

The One who made humans able to speak could give a donkey a human voice whenever he chose.

The donkey protested Balaam's cruelty.

God's righteousness protects even the weakest creatures from abuse; he can provide them with a voice or defend them himself.

At last Balaam's eyes were opened.

God has many ways of humbling a stubborn heart.

When our spiritual eyes are opened, we recognize how dangerous our sinful choices are and how much mercy there was in being stopped.

Balaam said, “I have sinned.”

Yet he did not seem to understand or admit the corruption of his own heart.

He was prepared to turn back only because he could not continue.

Some people abandon their sins only because their sins can no longer be carried out.

The angel made clear that Balaam would not merely fail to curse Israel: he would be compelled to bless the people.

That would bring God greater honor, and Balaam greater shame, than if he had returned home.

Balaam meets Balak (verses 36–41)

Balak complained that Balaam had not come sooner.

Balaam warned the king that he could not say whatever he wanted.

He sounded annoyed.

Yet he remained just as eager to please Balak as he had previously claimed to be eager to please God.

We desperately need to pray, “Our Father in heaven, do not lead us into temptation.”

We should watch over our own hearts.

Balaam shows how much knowledge a person may possess about God while still remaining without the saving grace of God.
classic_reading:
[Num.22.1-Num.22.14]
Chapter 22
Chapter Outline
Balak's fear of Israel, He sends for Balaam. | (1-14) |
Balaam goes to Balak. | (15-21) |
The opposition to Balaam by the way. | (22-35) |
Balaam and Balak meet. | (36-41) |
Verses 1-14
The king of Moab formed a plan to get the people of Israel cursed; that is, to set God against them, who had hitherto fought for them. He had a false notion, that if he could get some prophet to pray for evil upon them, and to pronounce a blessing upon himself and his forces, that then he should be able to deal with them. None had so great a reputation as Balaam; and Balak will employ him, though he send a great way for him. It is not known whether the Lord had ever spoken to Balaam, or by him, before this; though it is probable he had, and it is certain he did afterwards. Yet we have abundant proof that he lived and died a wicked man, an enemy to God and his people. And the curse shall not come upon us if there is not a cause, even though men utter it. To prevail with Balaam, they took the wages of unrighteousness, but God laid restraint upon Balaam, forbidding him to curse Israel. Balaam was no stranger to Israel's cause; so that he ought to have answered the messengers at once, that he would never curse a people whom God had blessed; but he takes a night's time to consider what he should do. When we parley with temptations, we are in great danger of being overcome. Balaam was not faithful in returning God's answer to the messengers. Those are a fair mark for Satan's temptation, who lessen Divine restraints; as if to go against God's law were only to go without his leave. The messengers also are not faithful in returning Balaam's answer to Balak. Thus many are abused by the flatteries of those about them, and are prevented from seeing their own faults and follies.
[Num.22.15-Num.22.21]
Verses 15-21
A second embassy was sent to Balaam. It were well for us, if we were as earnest and constant in prosecuting a good work, notwithstanding disappointments. Balak laid a bait, not only for Balaam's covetousness, but for his pride and ambition. How earnestly should we beg of God daily to mortify such desires in us! Thus sinners stick at no pains, spare no cost, and care not how low they stoop, to gratify their luxury, or their malice. Shall we then be unwilling to do what is right? God forbid! Balaam's convictions charged him to keep to the command of God; nor could any man have spoken better. But many call God theirs, who are not his, not truly because not only his. There is no judging men by their words; God knows the heart. Balaam's corruptions at the same time inclined him to go contrary to the command. He seemed to refuse the temptation; but he expressed no abhorrence of it. He had a strong desire to accept the offer, and hoped that God might give him leave to go. He had already been told what the will of God was. It is a certain evidence of the ruling of corruption in the heart, to beg leave to sin. God gave Balaam up to his own heart's lusts. As God sometimes denies the prayers of his people in love, so sometimes he grants the desires of the wicked in wrath.
[Num.22.22-Num.22.35]
Verses 22-35
We must not think, that because God does not always by his providence restrain men from sin, therefore he approves of it, or that it is not hateful to him. The holy angels oppose sin, and perhaps are employed in preventing it more than we are aware. This angel was an adversary to Balaam, because Balaam counted him his adversary; those are really our best friends, and we ought so to reckon them, who stop our progress in sinful ways. Balaam has notice of God's displeasure by the ass. It is common for those whose hearts are fully set in them to do evil, to push on violently, through the difficulties Providence lays in their way. The Lord opened the mouth of the ass. This was a great miracle wrought by the power of God. He who made man speak, could, when he pleased, make the ass to speak with man's voice. The ass complained of Balaam's cruelty. The righteous God does not allow the meanest or weakest to be abused; but they shall be able to speak in their own defence, or he will some way or other speak for them. Balaam at length has his eyes opened. God has many ways to bring down the hard and unhumbled heart. When our eyes are opened, we shall see the danger of sinful ways, and how much it was for our advantage to be crossed. Balaam seemed to relent; I have sinned; but it does not appear that he was sensible of this wickedness of his heart, or willing to own it. If he finds he cannot go forward, he will be content, since there is no remedy, to go back. Thus many leave their sins, only because their sins have left them. The angel declared that he should not only be unable to curse Israel, but should be forced to bless them: this would be more for the glory of God, and to his own confusion, than if he had turned back.
[Num.22.36-Num.22.41]
Verses 36-41
Balak has now nothing to complain of, but that Balaam did not come sooner. Balaam bids Balak not depend too much upon him. He seems to speak with vexation; but is really as desirous to please Balak, as ever he had pretended to be to please God. See what need we have to pray every day, Our Father which art in heaven, lead us not into temptation. Let us be jealous over our own hearts, seeing how far men may go in the knowledge of God, and yet come short of Divine grace.

Balaam blesses instead of cursing (verses 1–10)

With the camp of Israel clearly visible, Balaam ordered seven altars to be built, with a bull and a ram offered upon each.

What foolish superstition it is to imagine that human beings can command God to do what they want!

Through God's controlling power and love for Israel, the curse Balaam intended was turned into a blessing.

God intended to accomplish his own glory through Balaam, and therefore met him.

If the Lord could place words in the mouth of a man who was hostile to both God and Israel, he can certainly provide words for people who sincerely want to glorify him and build up his people.

The God who made Balaam's donkey speak now made the wicked prophet say what his own heart did not want to say.

The miracle was as great in one instance as in the other.

Balaam declared that Israel was safe.

He admitted that he could do only what God allowed.

He declared Israel blessed for being distinct from the nations, numerous enough to have dignity and strength, and secure in its future.

He also wished to enjoy the end of a righteous person's life.

Death comes to everyone, including the righteous.

We do well to consider our own deaths.

The righteous are blessed not only while living but also when dying.

Their death can therefore be more desirable than life itself.

But many people want the death of a righteous person without being willing to live a righteous life.

They want to be saints in heaven but not on earth.

Balaam expressed a wish, not a prayer rooted in genuine commitment.

He wanted the good end without caring about the way to reach it.

Others likewise quiet their consciences with promises of future change or false hopes, while neglecting the one path by which sinners can be justified before God.

Balaam blesses Israel again (verses 11–30)

Balak became angry with Balaam.

A wicked prophet was forced to acknowledge God's governing power, frustrating a wicked king.

For a second time, an intended curse became a blessing—this time even stronger and more extensive than before.

Human beings change their minds and break their promises.

God does not change his mind or withdraw his promises.

When Scripture speaks of God repenting, Henry explains that this means a change in the way he deals with people, not a change within God's own mind.

There was sin among Jacob's descendants, and the Lord saw it.

Yet it was not the kind of settled rebellion for which he was now abandoning them to destruction.

When people trust God's mercy, accept his salvation, refuse to indulge cherished sinful desires, and seek to honor him, they may be assured of acceptance in Christ and the forgiveness of their sins.

Think of the wonders of Providence and grace: redeeming love, forgiving mercy and the Spirit making people new!

Balak could no longer expect to destroy Israel.

Balaam now warned that Balak had more reason to fear destruction by Israel.

Because Balaam would not pronounce the curse Balak wanted, the king told him to say nothing.

Yet God's purposes prevail over every human scheme.

Balak and Balaam resolved to make another attempt, despite possessing no divine promise of success.

We, by contrast, have God's sure promises.

Let us persevere earnestly in prayer (Luke 18:1).
classic_reading:
[Num.23.1-Num.23.10]
Chapter 23
Chapter Outline
Balak's sacrifice, Balaam pronounces a blessing instead of a curse. | (1-10) |
Balak's disappointment, and second sacrifice, Balaam again blesses Israel. | (11-30) |
Verses 1-10
With the camps of Israel full in view, Balaam ordered seven altars to be built, and a bullock and a ram to be offered on each. Oh the sottishness of superstition, to imagine that God will be at man's beck! The curse is turned into a blessing, by the overruling power of God, in love to Israel. God designed to serve his own glory by Balaam, and therefore met him. If God put a word into the mouth of Balaam, who would have defied God and Israel, surely he will not be wanting to those who desire to glorify God, and to edify his people; it shall be given what they should speak. He who opened the mouth of the ass, caused the mouth of this wicked man to speak words as contrary to the desire of his heart, as those of the ass were to the powers of the brute. The miracle was as great in the one case as in the other. Balaam pronounces Israel safe. He owns he could do no more than God suffered him to do. He pronounces them happy in their distinction from the rest of the nations. Happy in their numbers, which made them both honourable and formidable. Happy in their last end. Death is the end of all men; even the righteous must die, and it is good for us to think of this with regard to ourselves, as Balaam does here, speaking of his own death. He pronounces the righteous truly blessed, not only while they live, but when they die; which makes their death even more desirable than life itself. But there are many who desire to die the death of the righteous, but do not endeavour to live the life of the righteous; gladly would they have an end like theirs, but not a way like theirs. They would be saints in heaven, but not saints on earth. This saying of Balaam's is only a wish, not a prayer; it is a vain wish, being only a wish for the end, without any care for the means. Many seek to quiet their consciences with the promise of future amendment, or take up with some false hope, while they neglect the only way of salvation, by which a sinner can be righteous before God.
[Num.23.11-Num.23.30]
Verses 11-30
Balak was angry with Balaam. Thus a confession of God's overruling power is extorted from a wicked prophet, to the confusion of a wicked prince. A second time the curse is turned into a blessing; and this blessing is both larger and stronger than the former. Men change their minds, and break their words; but God never changes his mind, and therefore never recalls his promise. And when in Scripture he is said to repent, it does not mean any change of his mind; but only a change of his way. There was sin in Jacob, and God saw it; but there was not such as might provoke him to give them up to ruin. If the Lord sees that we trust in his mercy, and accept of his salvation; that we indulge no secret lust, and continue not in rebellion, but endeavour to serve and glorify him; we may be sure that he looks upon us as accepted in Christ, that our sins are all pardoned. Oh the wonders of providence and grace, the wonders of redeeming love, of pardoning mercy, of the new-creating Spirit! Balak had no hope of ruining Israel, and Balaam showed that he had more reason to fear being ruined by them. Since Balaam cannot say what he would have him, Balak wished him to say nothing. But though there are many devices in man's heart, God's counsels shall stand. Yet they resolve to make another attempt, though they had no promise on which to build their hopes. Let us, who have a promise that the vision at the end shall speak and not lie, continue earnest in prayer, [Luke.18.1] Lu 18:1.

Balaam foretells Israel's happiness (verses 1–9)

Balaam was no longer expressing his own wishes.

He spoke words given by the Spirit who came upon him.

It is possible for someone's eyes to be opened while the heart remains closed.

People may receive spiritual knowledge without becoming holy.

Knowledge that only increases pride can serve to illuminate a person's road toward destruction.

The blessing resembled the earlier ones.

Balaam admired the beauty of Israel, whose righteous people were more excellent than their neighbors.

He spoke of Israel's fruitfulness and growth, dignity and advancement, power and victories.

He recalled the mighty things God had already done for the people.

He spoke of their courage and security.

The righteous can be as bold as lions without being aggressive toward others, because they rest safely in God's protection.

He also declared that the way other people treated Israel would matter to God himself.

The Lord regarded good or evil done to his people as good or evil done to him.

Balak sends Balaam away in anger (verses 10–14)

Balak's plan to bring a curse upon Israel had failed.

He became enraged at Balaam and expressed his frustration openly.

Balaam could answer that God had prevented him from speaking the curses he wanted to speak, and had compelled him to give blessings he did not want to give.

Balaam's final prophecies (verses 15–25)

Under the Spirit's prophetic power, Balaam announced Israel's future prosperity and far-reaching rule.

He boasted of having open eyes.

The prophets of earlier times were sometimes called seers.

Balaam had heard God's words.

But a person can hear the words of God without truly listening to God.

He claimed knowledge of the Most High.

Yet someone may possess extensive theological knowledge while remaining entirely without divine grace.

Balaam called God the Most High and the Almighty.

He seemed outwardly reverent, but lacked true love, fear and faith.

A person can advance very far in religious profession while never entering salvation.

Balaam's vision pointed to the great King who would be Israel's glory.

David partly fulfilled the pattern.

But the prophecy chiefly pointed to Jesus Christ, the promised Messiah.

Balaam would see Christ, but not in the way Job had seen his own Redeemer by faith.

He would see him from far away, without receiving him as his own.

When Christ returns in the clouds, everyone will see him.

Yet many will see him from a distance, as the rich man in torment saw Abraham.

The promised ruler would arise from Jacob and Israel as a Star and a Scepter.

The star spoke of his splendor and glory.

The scepter spoke of his power and royal authority.

Christ would reign not only over Israel but over the whole world.

Everyone will either willingly submit to his gracious royal rule or fall under his judgment.

Balaam also foretold what would happen to the Amalekites and Kenites, whose lands were nearby.

A nest high among the rocks cannot give permanent protection against God's purposes.

Henry understands the later prophecies to reach as far as the Greeks and Romans, showing that the rise and fall of kingdoms belongs to the Lord.

These upheavals would bring widespread destruction, leaving some survivors only as people snatched from a fire.

May God prepare us for the worst times!

Henry goes further in his confessional interpretation.

He understands Balaam as cursing Amalek as an early enemy of the church and Rome as its last enemy, and applies the latter not only to pagan Rome but also to papal Rome, which he associates with Antichrist and antichristian powers.

This is Henry's historical Protestant polemic and is preserved as his interpretation, not adopted as an independent modern editorial judgment.

What do we have that Balaam lacked?

Skill in public speaking, eloquent preaching or prayer, religious knowledge and even remarkable gifts cannot save anyone by themselves.

Balaam possessed such gifts, yet loved the rewards of wrongdoing and died an enemy of God.

Simple trust in the Redeemer's atoning blood and sanctifying grace, willing submission to God's will, and steady efforts to honor God and help his people may appear less impressive.

But those qualities truly accompany salvation.

No proud hypocrite possesses them, while even the weakest believer has something of them and prays daily for more.

Under the powerful influence of the Spirit of prophecy, Balaam foretold the future prosperity and extensive dominion of Israel. Balaam boasts that his eyes are open. The prophets were in old times called seers. He had heard the words of God, which many do who neither heed them, nor hear God in them. He knew the knowledge of the Most High. A man may be full of the knowledge of God, yet utterly destitute of the grace of God. He calls God the Most High and the Almighty. No man could seem to express a greater respect to God; yet he had no true fear of him, love to him, nor faith in him; so far a man may go toward heaven, and yet come short of it at last. Here is Balaam's prophecy concerning Him who should be the crown and glory of his people Israel; who is David in the type; but our Lord Jesus, the promised Messiah, is chiefly pointed at, and of him it is an illustrious prophecy. Balaam, a wicked man, shall see Christ, but shall not see him nigh; not see him as Job, who saw him as his Redeemer, and saw him for himself. When he comes in the clouds, every eye shall see him; but many will see him, as the rich man in hell saw Abraham, afar off. Here is a prophecy that looks as far forward as to the Greeks and Romans. He acknowledges all the revolutions of states and kingdoms to be the Lord's doing. These events will make such desolations, that scarcely any will escape. They that live then, will be as brands plucked out of the fire. May God fit us for the worst of times! Let us ask ourselves, Do we in knowledge, experience, or profession, excel Balaam? Israel is drawn into sin (verses 1–5)

The friendship of wicked people can be more dangerous than their open hostility.

Israel could not be overcome by enemies unless the people first yielded to the sinful desires within their own hearts.

No magical curse could defeat them in the way that worldly ambition, pleasure and temptation could.

The women of Moab and Midian enticed Israel into wrongdoing.

Those who draw others into sin may be our worst enemies, because nothing can harm us more seriously.

Israel's own sin accomplished what all Balaam's attempted curses had failed to do.

It brought God's judgment against the people.

Henry understands the outbreak of disease as a righteous consequence of serious prevailing sins.

Those who lead other people into such wrongdoing were to be publicly held accountable.

Phinehas acts against Zimri and Cozbi (verses 6–15)

Phinehas acted with courage, zeal and faith when he put Zimri and Cozbi to death in this historical judgment.

But Henry adds a decisive limitation.

This action must never be treated as a precedent for private revenge, religious persecution or unauthorized public punishment.

The exceptional action recorded in Israel's history gives no license to carry out violence against others today.

The judgment against Midian (verses 16–18)

The account does not say that any Midianites died from the plague that struck Israel.

God instead judged them through the sword of an enemy, not through the corrective rod used against his own children.

We must oppose whatever draws us toward sin (Matthew 5:29–30).

Anything that tempts us to wrongdoing should become painful and unwelcome to us, like a thorn in the flesh.

Those who follow Satan's pattern by cleverly enticing others into sin will face especially serious judgment.

The new census in Moab (verses 1–51)

Moses did not number Israel whenever he wished.

He did so only when the Lord commanded him.

This record lists not only Israel's tribes but also the families within them.

The total number of people was almost the same as at the earlier census at Mount Sinai.

Scripture specifically mentions the sons of Korah, who did not die as the children of Dathan and Abiram did.

They seem not to have joined even their own father in rebellion.

If we refuse to participate in other people's sins, we will not share the judgment brought upon them.

The division of Canaan (verses 52–56)

The inheritance was to be divided justly.

Larger tribes were to receive larger portions; smaller tribes, smaller portions.

Although the ruler's judgment played a part, the final outcome would be settled through God's providence.

The people should therefore accept his decision.

The Levites are counted separately (verses 57–62)

Levi was the tribe set apart for God.

It was therefore counted separately from the others.

The Levites were not included in the judgment that prevented the earlier generation from entering Canaan, with the exceptions of Caleb and Joshua.

The earlier generation has passed away (verses 63–65)

The judgment pronounced on the complaining generation had now been fulfilled (Numbers 14:29).

Not one of the people counted in the first census remained in the new census—except Caleb and Joshua.

This showed God's righteousness and the certainty of his warnings.

It also demonstrated his faithfulness in keeping the particular promises he had made to those two men.

Death brings enormous changes to families and nations.

Yet God's perfect wisdom, justice and truth govern every such change.

These truths should make us think seriously about the evil of sin, which brought death and so much destruction into the world.

Let us renew our repentance, seek forgiveness and value Christ's salvation.

Let us remember how frail we are, prepare for death and use the days given to us in serving our generation according to God's will.

The daughters of Zelophehad seek an inheritance (verses 1–11)

Zelophehad's five daughters were concerned about their inheritance.

Their father had died, and they had no brothers to inherit land on behalf of the family.

They trusted that God would keep his promise to give Canaan to Israel.

They wanted their own family to share in that promised inheritance.

They made their request modestly and honestly, without hidden resentment or complaining.

Henry sees three praiseworthy qualities in their conduct.

First, faith: they firmly believed God's power and promise concerning Canaan.

Second, earnest desire: they wanted both a place and a family name in the promised country, which pictured heaven.

Third, respect for their father: they treasured his memory after his death.

Their father had not been guilty of the particular rebellion that would exclude his children from a claim.

It comforts dying parents when, although they may have suffered because of their own sins, they do not know of any wrongdoing that will bring judgment upon their children.

God himself decided the matter.

His care extends beyond nations to individual households.

He governs their circumstances according to his wisdom.

The daughters' request was granted.

Those who seek an inheritance in the land of promise will obtain what they seek, with other blessings added.

Moses is warned that he will die (verses 12–14)

Moses had to die.

But God granted him the comfort of seeing the land he had promised Israel.

That sight of Canaan pointed toward Moses' believing expectation of a better, heavenly country.

Death would not finally cut him off.

It would bring him into the rest already enjoyed by the faithful patriarchs.

If we have lived as they lived and hope to reach the same peaceful end, we need not fear the passage through the valley of death.

Joshua is appointed Moses' successor (<reference osisRef="Num.27.15-Num.27.23" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 15–23</reference>)

Envious people dislike those who succeed them.

Moses was not like that.

We should pray and work for the next generation, so that faith may continue and flourish even after we are buried.

God appointed Joshua to succeed Moses.

Joshua had shown courage in the battle against Amalek, humility while assisting Moses, and faith and honesty when he opposed the unbelieving report of the spies.

God chose a man in whom his Spirit dwelt.

Joshua had the grace of the Spirit.

He feared God, hated greed and acted from principle.

He possessed the judgment and courage needed to lead.

He also had the Spirit's prophetic gift.

No one is fully qualified for service in Christ's church by human abilities alone.

The grace and gifts of the Holy Spirit are indispensable.

Joshua's succession also reminds us that the law was given through Moses.

Because of sin, the law cannot bring us into the heavenly inheritance.

Grace and truth come through Jesus Christ, who brings salvation to everyone who believes.

The daily offerings (verses 1–8)

God renewed the instructions concerning sacrifices.

Israel was entering a new generation, and the people would need to remain at peace with him while fighting their enemies.

The daily offering was called a continual burnt offering.

Christians are told to pray continually.

At the very least, we should offer solemn prayer and praise every morning and evening.

A particular instruction here is that the drink offering should use strong wine.

Henry understands this as a reminder to give God the best we possess.

The wine was also a figure of Christ's blood, remembered in the church through the wine of the Lord's Supper.

It also pictured the blood of martyrs, whose lives were poured out like a drink offering in the service of others' faith (Philippians 2:17).

The Sabbath and new moon offerings (verses 9–15)

Two additional lambs were to be offered each Sabbath, beyond the two offered daily.

Henry applies this to Christians by urging greater devotion on the Sabbath.

The purpose of Sabbath rest is to leave us freer for the holy work that should fill that day.

The monthly offerings showed gratitude for the renewal of God's earthly blessings.

Whenever Providence gives us a reason for joy, we should remember Christ's great sacrifice as the true foundation of all our spiritual happiness.

The New Moon celebrations also foreshadowed gospel worship (Isaiah 66:23).

Just as the moon receives light from the sun and is renewed through its influence, so the church receives light from Jesus Christ, the Sun of Righteousness.

Through him the church is continually renewed, especially under the gospel.

Passover and firstfruits offerings (<reference osisRef="Num.28.16-Num.28.31" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 16–31</reference>)

These repeated offerings remind us of the lasting effectiveness of Christ's sacrifice and of our continuing need to rely upon it.

Busy responsibilities, threatening circumstances or times of prosperity should never make us neglect prayer and worship.

They should give us even greater reason to seek the Lord's help and return thanks.

Our religious duties must be accompanied by repentance, faith in Jesus Christ and love toward him.

They should result in genuine holiness in our conduct toward others.

Otherwise God rejects even impressive public worship and lengthy devotion.

Christ is able to meet every need of every day, week, month and year, in every act of worship and every circumstance.

The obligation to fulfill a lawful vow (verses 1 and 2)

No human being can become obligated by a personal promise to do something that God's command already forbids.

A vow cannot make wrongdoing lawful.

In other matters, the rule is straightforward: we must not break our word.

We may change our minds later, but that does not release us from a valid promise.

Cases in which a vow could be canceled (verses 3–16)

The law describes two circumstances in which another member of the household could confirm or cancel a vow.

The first concerns a daughter living in her father's home. When the father learns of her vow, he may allow it to stand or cancel it.

The second concerns a wife.

If the husband approves the vow, even merely by remaining silent, the vow stands.

If he objects, the marriage obligation takes precedence under the household order established by this law, and the vow is canceled.

Henry understands this provision in terms of the authority of husbands and fathers within the family. In his explanation, a wife is to be subject to her husband as to the Lord, and a man is to govern his household.

Rather than allowing a religious vow to break the family bonds and authority he believes God appointed, Henry argues that divine law releases the person from that vow.

He concludes that God's ordinances are intended to preserve the welfare of families and societies, so that the families of the earth may enjoy blessing.

Two cases of vows are determined. The case of a daughter in her father's house. When her vow comes to his knowledge, it is in his power either to confirm it or do it away. The law is plain in the case of a wife. If her husband allows her vow, though only by silence, it stands. If he disallows it, her obligation to her husband takes place of it; for to him she ought to be in subjection, as unto the Lord. The Divine law consults the good order of families. It is fit that every man should bear rule in his own house, and have his wife and children in subjection; rather than that this great rule should be broken, or any encouragement be given to inferior relations to break those bonds asunder, God releases the obligation even of a solemn vow. So much does religion secure the welfare of all societies; and in it the families of the earth have a blessing.
